title: Twenty million voices
teaches: The Doppler shift and how horseshoe bats lower their call to keep the echo in their sharpest hearing, and how bats in a crowd avoid jamming each other, or jam on purpose
summary: **Bracken Cave's emergence shows on weather radar.** Millions of Mexican free-tailed bats leave over two to three hours on a summer evening and spread across the radar as a growing ring.
**Motion changes pitch.** When a source and a listener draw together the pitch heard rises, and when they draw apart it falls.
**An echo's shift is doubled.** A bat flying toward a target hears its echo raised by about twice its speed over the speed of sound: 2.4 kHz at 5 m/s and 83 kHz.

**Horseshoe bats have an acoustic fovea.** Their ears give a band only a few hundred hertz wide, near 83 kHz in the greater horseshoe bat, with far more of the inner ear given to it than to any other band.
**They lower their call to keep the echo there.** Schnitzler found in 1968 that a flying horseshoe bat drops its call by just enough that the echo lands within about 0.1 to 0.2 kHz of the same note.
**Compensation is not how bats avoid each other.** The crowd problem is jamming: a neighbour's call is far louder than one's own echo.
**Free-tailed bats move their pitch away from a neighbour's.** In a fraction of a second, so each listens in a band of its own.
**Some jam on purpose.** Free-tailed bats have a wavering call that covers a rival's buzz and makes it miss the moth.

blocks.text: Bracken Cave lies in the dry limestone hills north-east of San Antonio, Texas. Each spring female Mexican free-tailed bats, *Tadarida brasiliensis*, fly up from Mexico to bear their pups in it, and by midsummer it holds what is often put at 15 to 20 million bats, the largest gathering of mammals known anywhere. Counts made with thermal cameras in the 2000s came in lower, but even the low counts are in the millions.[^counts]

Toward evening the bats begin to spiral up out of the cave mouth in a dense column, and they keep coming for two to three hours. They climb a kilometre or more and fan out across south Texas to feed on moths through the night. The column is thick enough to show on the National Weather Service's radar at New Braunfels, some 30 km away, as a patch of echo that swells from the cave and widens into a ring as the bats fly off in every direction, much like a small storm that appears out of a clear sky.[^radar]

blocks.caption: An evening emergence from Bracken Cave as the radar would see it, in a simple model: bats leave over two and a half hours and spread from the cave at about 30 km an hour. Darker means more bats in the air. Not real radar data.

blocks.text: Every one of those bats is calling. A free-tailed bat in open air gives long, nearly steady calls of about 25 kHz, and in the column it has many neighbours within a few metres, all calling at much the same pitch. Each must pick its own faint echoes out of that din. That is the second of two problems in this lesson. The first concerns a single bat, flying alone, whose own speed puts its echoes out of tune.

An ambulance's siren drops in pitch as it passes. Pitch is how often the crests of a sound wave reach the ear, and motion changes that. A siren sends out crests at a steady rate, each spreading from wherever the siren was when it left. If the siren moves toward a listener, each new crest starts a little closer than the last, so the crests arrive bunched together, more of them each second, and the pitch heard is higher. Behind the siren the crests are stretched apart and the pitch is lower. This is the **Doppler shift**, after the Austrian physicist Christian Doppler, who proposed it in 1842.

It works the other way round too. A listener running toward a still source meets the crests sooner than they would have arrived, so again more crests reach the ear each second and the pitch rises. In both cases the size of the shift depends on the speed compared with the speed of sound, 343 metres a second: something moving at 1% of that shifts the pitch by about 1% on each trip the sound makes.

blocks.caption: Crests of a steady call, from a moving source, to a moving listener, and back off a wall. The speeds are exaggerated so the bunching shows; a real bat flies at about 1.5% of the speed of sound.
blocks.task: Try the source, the listener and the wall, each with some speed

blocks.text: A bat flying toward a wall is both: a moving source on the way out and a moving listener on the way back. The wall is a listener with the source coming toward it, so it receives the [[call|call]] already raised in pitch. The wall then sends back exactly what it receives, as an [[echo|echo]], and the bat, still flying forward, runs into the returning crests and raises their pitch a second time. For a bat flying at speed *v*, the echo comes back higher by about 2*v* divided by the speed of sound. For a greater horseshoe bat, the bat of the next part, calling near 83 kHz at 5 metres a second, that is 2 × 5 ÷ 343 × 83,000, about 2,400 Hz, or 2.4 kHz.

To most bats 2.4 kHz hardly matters. A big brown bat's call sweeps across tens of kilohertz, and its ear hears all of them about equally well. The greater horseshoe bat, *Rhinolophus ferrumequinum*, is different. As lesson 3 showed, it gives long calls held on one steady note, near 83 kHz, and its ear is built around that note. A stretch of its inner ear many times longer than any other band of the same width gets is given over to a band only a few hundred hertz wide just above the note, and the nerve cells there are very sharply tuned. This band is the bat's **acoustic fovea**, named after the small spot in the centre of our eye where we see most sharply.[^fovea]

Hans-Ulrich Schnitzler, a young German zoologist, recorded greater horseshoe bats in flight and published what he found in 1968. Hanging still, a bat called at its usual note. In flight it called lower, and the faster it flew the lower it called, by just enough that the echo came back at the note it used when still. The bats were keeping their echoes inside the fovea, to within about 0.1 to 0.2 kHz, adjusting call by call as their speed changed. This is **Doppler shift compensation**.

blocks.caption: A greater horseshoe bat's hearing across the pitches near its call, with the acoustic fovea shaded. Set the bat's speed and turn its compensation on and off.
blocks.task: Guess, see the echo miss, then bring it back

blocks.text: The prize is a sharp view of anything that flutters. Against a steady echo from leaves and twigs, an insect's beating wings add tiny, rhythmic flickers to the echo. Each wingbeat swings the wing toward the bat and away, so the echo from it rises and falls in pitch by its own Doppler shift, and it flashes louder when the wing faces the bat. An ear tuned this finely picks the flickers out. A horseshoe bat hanging on a twig, scanning for passing insects, can tell a moth from a leaf by its wingbeat alone. In the mustached bat, which also lowers its call this way, Suga found brain cells tuned to particular Doppler shifts beside the delay-tuned cells of the last lesson, so the same strip of cortex reports how far away a target is and how fast it is closing.

None of this helps a free-tailed bat in the Bracken column. Its problem is not its own speed but its neighbours. A call shouted by a bat 2 metres away reaches it far louder than its own echo from a moth 5 metres away, which has spread out, lost energy to the air and bounced off something small. If the neighbour calls in the band where it listens for its echo, the echo is lost. Engineers call this **jamming**.

In 2007 Erin Gillam and her colleagues played recorded calls at free-tailed bats hunting in the wild. A bat hearing another call close to its own pitch moved its own call away, up if the intruder was below, down if above, within a fraction of a second. Each bat then had a band to itself. Electric fish in South American rivers solve the same problem by shifting the frequency of their electric fields away from a neighbour's.[^fish]

blocks.caption: Bat A chasing a moth, with bat B close by. Below, what A hears by pitch: its own faint echo, its listening band (dashed), and B's much louder call. Bar heights show loudness. Move A's call and its echo and listening band move with it.
blocks.task: Move A's call until it hears its echo clearly

blocks.text: Bats can also jam on purpose. In 2014 Aaron Corcoran and William Conner reported that free-tailed bats hunting the same patch of sky sometimes give a special social call, a call whose pitch swings rapidly up and down across the pitches of a rival's feeding buzz, timed to the moment the rival closes on a moth. When they played the call at hunting bats, the bats missed far more of their catches. Moths had been shown jamming bats five years earlier, in self-defence (the next lesson); this was the first evidence of one bat jamming another, and of jamming used to steal food. Turn on B's jamming call in the figure and there is nowhere for bat A to move: the sweep covers every pitch its buzz uses.

blocks.caption: Five questions on Doppler and crowds
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: A bat flies toward a still wall and calls on one steady note. How does the pitch of the echo compare with the call?
choices: Higher, shifted once on the way out and again on the way back
Higher, but only by the shift on the way out, since the wall is still
The same, because the wall does not move
items.why: The wall receives crests bunched by the bat's motion and sends them back, and the bat then runs into them. The echo is raised by about twice the bat's speed over the speed of sound.

items.ask: A horseshoe bat speeds up from 2 to 6 metres a second while hunting. What does it do with its call?
choices: Lowers it further, so the echo still lands on the same note
Raises it, so the call is easier to hear above the wind of its flight
Keeps it on the same note, and listens a little higher for the echo
items.why: The faster it flies, the more its echo is raised, and its sharpest hearing is fixed in a narrow band. By calling lower it brings the echo back into that band.

items.ask: Why does a horseshoe bat need its echo inside such a narrow band of hearing?
choices: Its sharpest tuning is there, fine enough to pick out the flicker of an insect's wingbeats in the echo
Echoes outside the band cannot reach its inner ear at all, so it would be deaf to them
Its call can only be made on that note, so the echo has to match it to be heard
items.why: The acoustic fovea is a few hundred hertz wide with very sharply tuned cells. A steady echo with fluttering wings in it stands out there, which is how the bat tells a moth from a leaf.

items.ask: Two free-tailed bats hunt side by side, calling at the same pitch. Why does the second bat's call matter so much to the first?
choices: It reaches the first bat far louder than the first bat's own echo from a distant moth
It changes the pitch of the first bat's echo through the Doppler shift
It travels faster than the first bat's echo and arrives before it
items.why: An echo from a small insect several metres away is very faint, while a neighbour's call from a couple of metres is loud. If they share a band, the echo is lost.

items.ask: A free-tailed bat hears another calling just below its own pitch. What does it most likely do?
choices: Move its own call up, away from the other's
Move its own call down to match the other's
Fly faster, so the Doppler shift moves its echo out of the way
items.why: Free-tailed bats shift their calls away from a neighbour's within a fraction of a second, so each listens in its own band. That is jamming avoidance, a different thing from Doppler compensation.

counts.title: Counting a column
counts.text: The traditional figures came from estimating the size of the column and how fast bats moved in it. In 2008 Margrit Betke and colleagues counted bats leaving several Texas caves frame by frame in thermal camera video, with a computer, and found totals several times lower than the old estimates. Numbers also vary from year to year and through the summer.

radar.title: Weather radar and bats
radar.text: The NEXRAD radars send out pulses of radio waves and time their echoes, the same trick as a bat's on a different scale. A dense flight of bats or birds reflects enough to show. The radars are also Doppler radars: they measure the shift in the echo's frequency to tell how fast the targets are moving toward or away from them.

fovea.title: The fovea in the ear
fovea.text: Different pitches set different parts of the inner ear's coiled membrane vibrating. In the greater horseshoe bat a long stretch of it responds only to the narrow band near 83 kHz, and the exact note differs a little from bat to bat and region to region. Each bat compensates to its own note.

fish.title: Jamming avoidance in fish
fish.text: Weakly electric knifefish such as *Eigenmannia* sense their surroundings through a steady electric field. When two fish with nearly the same frequency meet, each shifts away from the other, a behaviour described in the 1960s and worked out in detail by Walter Heiligenberg. Fish were found doing it decades before bats.
